FACT SHEET

RECOMMENDATION: "Battery not yet"
- The payback falls outside at least one limit of the decision rule.
- Battery size assessed: 10 kWh of usable capacity.

THE DECISION RULE
A battery is recommended now only if its payback falls within both the battery's warranty and the years the household expects to stay in its home.
- The battery's payback: 12.5 years.
- Warranty: 10 years. FAILED: the payback is outside it by 2.5 years.
- Expected years in the home: 12 years. FAILED: the payback is outside it by 0.5 years.

HOW THE SAVING AND THE PAYBACK ARE WORKED OUT
annual saving = kWh moved × (value on release − cost to store ÷ efficiency) + demand saving
payback = (installed price − rebate) ÷ annual saving
- kWh the battery moves in a year: 2,880 kWh
- value on release, the average rate where the battery discharged: 30.00 c/kWh
- cost to store, the average cost of what it charged with (the import rate when charging from the grid, the feed-in tariff forgone when charging from solar): 5.00 c/kWh
- round-trip efficiency: 90%
- cost to store per kWh delivered, after losses (cost to store ÷ efficiency): 5.56 c/kWh
- margin on each kWh moved (value on release − cost per kWh delivered): 24.44 c/kWh
- demand saving: $0
- annual saving: $704
- installed price: $11,390; rebate: $2,584; net outlay: $8,806
- payback: 12.5 years
- What limits the battery's value: battery capacity and available surplus. It was full on 102 days of the year, with 407 kWh worth serving left unmet.

NOW AGAINST LATER: the running position, savings to date minus the net outlay
- Year 1: -$8,102 (the net outlay of $8,806, less the first year's saving of $704)
- Year 2: -$7,398
- Year 3: -$6,694
- Year 4: -$5,990
- Year 5: -$5,286
- Year 6: -$4,582
- Year 7: -$3,878
- Year 8: -$3,174
- Year 9: -$2,469
- Year 10: -$1,765
- Year 11: -$1,061
- Year 12: -$357
- Crossover, the first year the position is no longer negative: year 13
- Every year is at today's prices: no growth.

WHAT THE PAYBACK LEAVES OUT (not priced)
- independence from retailer price rises. THE HOUSEHOLD SAID THIS MATTERS TO IT. Prices are held at today's rates, so protection from future rises is not valued.
- backup power in an outage. The payback counts bill savings only; keeping essentials running in a blackout is not valued.
- evening peak relief. Discharging in the evening eases the network's peak; nothing in the household's number pays for that.
- battery wear. Wear decides which kWh are worth moving (2.0 c/kWh) but is not subtracted from the saving.
- outliving the warranty. The payback (12.5 years) runs past the 10-year warranty, so the battery may not last long enough to break even.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ASSESSMENT: each found by re-running the model
- Battery price (installed, before the rebate), now $11,390: at $9,621 the answer changes from "Battery not yet" to "Battery now". ADVICE CHANGES: YES. The battery's payback at $9,621 is 10.0 years.
- Feed-in tariff, now 5.0 c/kWh: no change in the answer anywhere from 0.0 c/kWh to 15.0 c/kWh, the range searched; it stays "Battery not yet".
- Flat rate (c/kWh added to it), now +0.0 c/kWh: at +6.2 c/kWh the answer changes from "Battery not yet" to "Battery now". ADVICE CHANGES: YES. The battery's payback at +6.2 c/kWh is 10.0 years.
- Adding solar (kW of panels): not applicable, because the household already has 6.6 kW.

ASSUMPTIONS THAT SHAPED THE RESULT
- battery installed price: $11,390 (source: config/batteries.yaml: $4,250 + $714 × 10 kWh; dated 2026-09-26)
- rebate: $2,584 (source: config/incentives.yaml: deeming factor 6.8 for installs from 2026-05-01 to 2026-12-31, at $38.00 per STC; the range is the rebate at $33.00 to $40.00 per STC; dated 2026-09-26); plausible range $2,244 to $2,720
- round-trip efficiency: 90% (source: config/batteries.yaml; dated 2026-09-26); plausible range 85% to 92%
- marginal wear cost: 2.0 c/kWh (source: config/batteries.yaml; dated 2026-09-26); plausible range 0.5 c/kWh to 5.0 c/kWh
- warranty: 10 years (source: config/batteries.yaml; dated 2026-09-26)
- electricity prices: held at today's rates: no growth (source: tariff generic_flat_2026 (config/tariffs.yaml))
- planning horizon: 24 hours (source: config/assumptions.yaml); plausible range 24 hours to 48 hours
- solar output, June against December: 0.5 (source: config/assumptions.yaml); plausible range 0.45 to 0.75
- cloudy days: 25% of days at 40% output, evenly spaced (optimistic) (source: config/assumptions.yaml)
- time of day, from the form (the bill has no window split): both_out_weekdays: weekdays use the out_during_the_day shape, 14% of the day between 9:00 and 16:00 (source: config/assumptions.yaml); plausible range 10% to 20%

THE HOUSEHOLD'S STATED PRIORITIES
- a lower bill: decided the answer: the bill saving is what the payback measures
- independence from retailer price rises: stated but not priced, so it did not move the answer (see not_priced)

HOW CERTAIN THIS IS
- The bill has one flat rate and no time-of-day split, so how this household's use falls across the day comes from its form answers, not its bills. This result is materially less certain than one built from a time-of-use bill.
- The figures come from one representative year, carried forward at today's prices. A different year's use or prices would give different figures: they are not a forecast.

Write the justification for the household this fact sheet describes.
reply:
Our recommendation for your home is "Battery not yet". The main reason is that a 10 kWh battery would take 12.5 years to pay for itself, which is longer than it is expected to last under warranty and longer than you expect to stay in your home.

A battery is recommended now only if its payback falls within both the battery's warranty and the years you expect to stay. The warranty is 10 years, so the payback misses it by 2.5 years. You expect to stay 12 years, so it misses that by 0.5 years.

Here is how the saving is worked out. The battery would move 2,880 kWh in a year. Each kWh it releases is worth 30.00 c/kWh on average. Storing it costs 5.00 c/kWh, mostly the feed-in tariff you give up by storing solar instead of exporting it. With a round-trip efficiency of 90%, that cost becomes 5.56 c/kWh for each kWh delivered, which leaves a margin of 24.44 c/kWh. There is no demand saving, at $0, so the annual saving is $704. The installed price is $11,390, less a rebate of $2,584, for a net outlay of $8,806. Dividing that outlay by the annual saving gives the payback of 12.5 years. The battery's value is limited by its capacity and by how much surplus solar you have. It was full on 102 days of the year, leaving 407 kWh worth serving unmet.

After year 1 you would be behind by -$8,102. By year 10 you would still be at -$1,765. Your position would first stop being negative in year 13. All of these figures use today's prices, with no growth.

The payback leaves several things out. You told us that independence from retailer price rises matters to you. Because prices are held at today's rates, protection from future rises is not valued. The payback also does not value backup power during a blackout, or the easing of the evening peak on the network. Battery wear of 2.0 c/kWh is not subtracted from the saving. There is also a risk that the battery may not last past its warranty long enough to break even.

Two changes would move the answer to "Battery now". One is an installed price of $9,621, which would bring the payback to 10.0 years. The other is your flat rate rising by +6.2 c/kWh, which would also give a payback of 10.0 years. We checked feed-in tariffs from 0.0 c/kWh to 15.0 c/kWh, and none of them changed the answer.

Three assumptions matter most. The first is that prices stay at today's rates. The second is the rebate, which could plausibly range from $2,244 to $2,720. The third is how your use falls across the day. Your bill has a single flat rate, so this comes from your form answers, which put 14% of your use between 9:00 and 16:00, within a plausible range of 10% to 20%. Because of this, the result is materially less certain than one built from a time-of-use bill. It is also based on one representative year, so it is not a forecast.
